title: Repeated evolution of high-elevation occupation in tropical lizards
content:
Abstract
Since Darwin and Humboldt, researchers have sought to understand how species adapt to elevation. Although tropical reptiles are typically most diverse in warm lowlands, many lineages have occupied highlands, but how often remains unclear: high-elevation species across multiple mountain ranges could reflect a single occupation event followed by diversification, or repeated occupation events with limited diversification. We tested these alternatives in anole lizards, using climatic and distributional data for 303 species and cold tolerance (CTmin) data for 64 species. Highlands have been occupied many times, though considerably less often than the reverse transition, and both dispersal among mountain ranges and climatic niche shifts are distributed nonrandomly across the phylogeny. Lowland-highland transitions did not coincide with shifts in the rate of trait evolution for either cold tolerance or minimum thermal niche. Instead, highland lineages showed stronger selection toward a colder optimum for minimum thermal niche, consistent with climatic niche conservatism in montane environments. Cold tolerance showed no such shift, indicating a decoupling between the climate lineages experience and the evolution of a physiological trait expected to track it. Overall, repeated mountain occupation has reshaped climatic niche evolution in Anolis, whereas cold tolerance has followed a comparatively stable, elevation-independent trajectory.
